title: How the Harlemites broke up and Freddy went to Holland
summary: The band lasted about six months for the recordings and Pleyel, then the players refused to leave their jobs; Johnson took another group to The Hague and Pete du Conge threw him out of Bricktop's.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: Well, how long did the band go on, before it broke up?
Well, we stayed together for -- just to make those recordings, 'cause after, after we finished the recordings, that's when we were supposed to go on the road.
That was what -- just like -- only until the band could --
No, that was six months.
Six months, that was all it was.

Yeh, we played at Salle de Pleyel, six months, and when they made all the bookings and everything else, they had no band, the boys refused to leave their jobs. They had no bands. Did I tell you about Freddy yet? He signed a contract -- I don't know
Briggs
whether Canetti was in on the deal, but he signed a contract for The Hague, in Amsterdam -- no, The Hague in Holland, at Tabariss Cabaret, dancehall cabaret.
He took most of the orchestra with me, but he knew I wasn't going. He knew it was finished, that I was not going to leave my job.
I still had my Ciro's job going, and I did not intend to go after I found out what was what. Yet, he proposed me.

And he went. He had taken another trumpet player and he went, and the following day I had a phone call from Mr. Brauer(7) who was the proprietor of the place, asking me, -- he said, "What happened?" "Mr. Johnson said that you were ill, and that you would be here in about a week or so, as soon as you're better."
And I said, there's no question, I said, "Mr. Johnson knew that the orchestra had folded." I said, "You don't have two men
Briggs

of the original orchestra with Mr. Johnson." I said, "But, if you're satisfied with it, just go ahead." So you see, those are the things -- it's a pity, 'cause we did something, when we had the first prize, awarded first prize in 1935, for "Best Recording of the Year." The world over. With those two numbers -- did I tell you, "Harlem Bound," and "Harlem Madness".
Okay, let me just try and get this straight, now.
When that thing broke up -- you were still recording into 1934 then?
Yes, uh huh.
So you made a first record in '33. And then most of the rest of these?
Yes, yes.
I see. But you were still speaking with Freddy?
Oh, yes, we were
Briggs

still -- surely, yes, but then he went to Holland. He went to Holland because Bricktop -- Pete du Conge, also found out, 'cause Sterling Conaway kept it more or less secret, you see, and didn't want any dissensions.
Pete only found out at the last moment, and he had taken it in a pretty bad manner. He told his wife, 'If you don't throw him out, I'll throw him out.' That's when Freddie decided to go to Holland.
So Freddie left and went to Holland?
Yes, went to Holland, yes.
Well, it's just one of those things that happened. But when he told me, I'm glad he said, 'If I had my life to live over, I would do it differently.'
Yeh.
